lead: AJAX means Asynchronous JavaScript and XML. It is the trick of asking the server for data after the page has already loaded, then writing the reply into one part of the page. The page does not reload. Before AJAX, every click that needed new data sent the whole page to the server and got a whole new page back. With AJAX a small request goes out in the background and only one element changes. Search suggestions, a college portal's marks lookup, UPI balance refresh and IRCTC seat availability all run on this.
prereq: You need: 3.4 for writing into the page, and 3.6 for call-backs, so you understand that the reply arrives later.

sections.h3: The path from page to server and back

blocks.text: AJAX stands for Asynchronous JavaScript and XML. The name is old — XML was the usual reply format when the term was coined — but the idea is simple: ask the server for data after the page has loaded, and patch one part of the page with the reply.

Asynchronous is the important word. The browser sends the request and does not wait for it. The user keeps typing or scrolling, and a call-back function runs when the reply arrives. 3.6 explains how that call-back is queued.

items: Create an XMLHttpRequest object. It is the browser's built-in messenger; your JavaScript never opens a socket itself.
Call open() to set the HTTP method and the URL, then send() to transmit.
The web server receives the request (HTTP is in Unit 1, Internet, Web and HTTP), runs its code, and replies with a status code and a body.
The XHR object receives the reply and calls your function. You read the body, parse it, and write the result into the DOM with textContent (3.4). The page never reloaded.

blocks.text: Create one with new XMLHttpRequest(). Three calls then set it up.

items: open(method, url, async) — method is 'GET' or 'POST', url is the endpoint, async is true for AJAX. Passing false blocks the whole page until the reply arrives, so almost nobody does it.
setRequestHeader(name, value) — adds a request header. A form-encoded POST needs Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
send(body) — sends it. GET sends null; POST sends the encoded string, for example name=Ravi&marks=65.

blocks.text: readyState counts how far the exchange has got.

head: readyState
Name
Meaning
rows: status line and headers have arrived

blocks.text: status is the HTTP status of the reply: 200 OK, 404 not found, 500 server error. readyState 4 only says the exchange is over; you must check both.

Older code assigns onreadystatechange = function () { ... } and tests readyState === 4 inside it. Newer browsers add onload (reply arrived) and onerror (network failed). Prefer onload and onerror in new code; expect onreadystatechange in exams.
responseText holds the body as a string. responseXML holds a parsed DOM when the reply is XML — see 3.8. Setting responseType = 'json' makes the browser parse JSON into response for you.
GET reads, POST writes. Use GET when the call only fetches data, because GET replies can be cached and bookmarked. Use POST when data changes on the server or the payload is long.
JSON is JavaScript Object Notation, a text format with three building blocks: objects {key: value}, arrays [a, b, c], and values (string, number, true, false, null). Its syntax has hard rules.

items: Every key is a double-quoted string.
Strings use double quotes, never single quotes.
No comma after the last item of an object or array.
No comments, no functions, no undefined, no NaN.

blocks.text: Two functions convert between text and live values. JSON.stringify(value) returns text, which is what you send to a server. JSON.parse(text) returns a value, which is what you do to responseText. Malformed text makes JSON.parse throw a SyntaxError, so wrap it in try/catch when an error page may come back instead of data.

blocks.text: fetch() is the modern promise-based call:

fetch does not reject on a 404 — check response.ok yourself. r.json() already parses, so never pass its result to JSON.parse. CORS in one line: a script may only read a reply from another origin (scheme + host + port) if that server sends an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. The server that answers these calls is built in Unit 6, Node.js, Express and Databases.

figure.caption: Every box is one readyState value from the worked example, and the call-back fires on all of them. The guard returns on 1, 2 and 3; only at readyState 4 with status 200 does the code parse the JSON and write Asha: 72 into #out.

spec.title: Worked example: readyState 0 to 4
spec.aria: The XMLHttpRequest object moves down through readyState 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4; the call-back fires at each step but the guard returns on 1, 2 and 3, and only at readyState 4 with status 200 does the code parse the JSON and write Asha: 72 into the page.

examples.question: A server returns [{"name":"Asha","marks":72}] at /api/marks.json. Write the XMLHttpRequest code that fetches it and writes 'Asha: 72' into <div id='out'>. List the readyState values the code passes through, and say what it does if the server answers 404.
steps: new XMLHttpRequest() creates the object. readyState is 0 (UNSENT).
open('GET', '/api/marks.json', true) sets the request. readyState becomes 1 (OPENED). Nothing has left the browser yet.
Assigning onreadystatechange registers the call-back. onerror covers a dead network.

send(null) transmits. readyState becomes 2 (HEADERS_RECEIVED) when the status line and headers arrive, 3 (LOADING) while the body streams in, and 4 (DONE) when it is complete. So the code passes 1 → 2 → 3 → 4; it never sees 0 again after send().
Each change fires the call-back. The guard 'if (xhr.readyState !== 4) return;' makes it do nothing on 1, 2 and 3.
At readyState 4 with status 200, responseText is exactly [{"name":"Asha","marks":72}]. JSON.parse turns that string into an array holding one object.
data[0].name is 'Asha' and data[0].marks is 72, so the div shows Asha: 72.
If the server answers 404, status is 404 while readyState is still 4. The status check writes 'Error 404' into the div and the JSON.parse line never runs, so no HTML error page is parsed as data.
examples.answer: The div shows Asha: 72 after readyState 4 with status 200, and shows Error 404 if the server answers 404.
examples.check:
import json
body = '[{"name":"Asha","marks":72}]'
data = json.loads(body)
print(data[0]['marks'])

traps: Updating the page on readyState 4 alone without checking status === 200, so a 404 page's HTML lands inside your div.
Thinking readyState 4 means success. It only means the exchange finished; status carries the outcome.
Reversing JSON.parse and JSON.stringify. stringify goes object → text (sending); parse goes text → object (receiving).
Calling JSON.parse on what r.json() already returned. r.json() gives a Promise of an object, not text.
Expecting fetch() to reject on 404. It resolves; you must test response.ok. Only network failures reject.
Writing single quotes or a trailing comma inside a JSON string. JSON.parse throws SyntaxError; it never repairs the text.

quiz.q: Expand AJAX and state what the 'A' means in practice.
quiz.a: Asynchronous JavaScript and XML. The request is sent without blocking the page; a call-back handles the reply when it arrives.

quiz.q: List the five readyState values of XMLHttpRequest with their names.
Why must the code check status as well as readyState?
quiz.a: A 404 or 500 also reaches readyState 4, with a body that is not your data. Status tells success (200) from failure, so both checks are needed before parsing.

quiz.q: Write one valid JSON line holding name 'Ravi', subjects 3, and marks [65, 70, 58].
XHR code does JSON.parse(xhr.responseText) with no status check and the server replies 404 with the body Not Found. What happens?
quiz.a: readyState 4 fires the call-back, JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError because Not Found is not JSON, the rest of the call-back is skipped and the div is not updated. Fix: test status first, or wrap the parse in try/catch.

quiz.q: A page works on http://localhost:3000 but its fetch to http://localhost:5000/api/fails in the browser console. Explain.
quiz.a: Different port means a different origin, so the request is cross-origin. The browser sends it but blocks the script from reading the reply unless the server returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin for that origin. The route itself is fine.

quiz.q: Why does passing async = false to open() defeat the purpose of AJAX?
quiz.a: False makes send() block the single JavaScript thread until the reply arrives. The page freezes, events queue up, and the user cannot type or scroll. AJAX's value is that the page stays live while the request travels, which needs async = true and a call-back.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most production code no longer touches XMLHttpRequest directly: fetch(), Axios and framework HTTP clients wrap it, and data libraries add caching, retries and loading states on top. XML replies still appear in SOAP and banking integrations, so the responseXML path still matters. Real-time needs go further, to WebSockets and Server-Sent Events, which keep one connection open instead of asking again. Search next: Fetch API streams, AbortController, Server-Sent Events, HTTP caching headers.
